oral-bioavailability outcome.

votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Glucose, a small polar sugar with active absorption, had oral bioavailability estimates of 0.722 in healthy subjects (C16), 0.843 in type 1 diabetic patients (C10), and 38% in hypoglycemic children (C15), all at or above the 20% threshold.

Mannitol, a highly polar sugar alcohol, showed absolute oral bioavailability of 0.228 at 150 g and about 20% at 100 g (C01, C06, C09, C17), and sorbitol showed 0.36–0.38 in shunted patients (C03, C19), indicating that small polyhydroxy compounds can meet the F ≥ 20% threshold despite low passive permeability.

Propylene glycol, a small polyol, was inferred to have very high or close-to-complete oral bioavailability (C13, C28, C29), providing additional support that small polar polyhydroxy compounds can be well absorbed.

New L2 records reinforce the same pattern: mannitol oral bioavailability was about 20% in man (C32), mannitol fraction absorbed was ~0.5 (C33), sorbitol bioavailability was 0.27 in cirrhotic patients (C24), and glucose bioavailability was 57.4% in red wattlebirds (C23).

Gemcitabine's low oral bioavailability (10%, range 5–17%; rat solution 9.86%; low rat exposure) is attributed to first-pass metabolism by cytidine deaminase and high first-pass clearance (C07, C18, C20, C21, C26, C30), a mechanism not applicable to ascorbic acid; these low outcomes therefore do not transfer.
BMOV, a maltol complex, had absolute oral bioavailability of 28.1–33.7% in rats (C27, C31), providing only weak supportive context because it is a different metal complex rather than ascorbic acid.
C25 (glibenclamide relative bioavailability) and C34 (relative glucose bioavailability between beverage types) are not absolute F ≥ 20% threshold evidence for ascorbic acid.

evidence_gaps: No direct ascorbic acid oral bioavailability record is present in the supplied cards.
Dose dependence of ascorbic acid absorption is not captured; active transport saturation could alter F at high doses.
Active transport (e.g., SVCT1/2) contribution is inferred from the query prior caveat, not from a measured record.
Transfer from glucose/mannitol/sorbitol/propylene glycol contexts is qualitative; species, patient status, and doses differ.
